*Reliable Measurement of Teachers' Instructional Practices with LLM Classifiers: Coefficients and Selection Criteria for Low-Inference Count-Based Systems*

## Abstract

Organizations increasingly use large language models to score human behavior at scale, but validation typically stops at agreement with expert labels — which measures classification accuracy, not reliability: whether scores rank people consistently across replications of the measurement procedure. This study develops a measurement model for scores built by applying a fixed LLM classifier to counts of behaviors across occasions, here teachers' instructional moves across lessons. Extending generalizability theory to the distinctive error structure of an LLM rater — which, unlike a human rater, applies the same systematic scoring tendencies on every occasion — the paper derives the reliability coefficient for classifier-based prevalence scores, decomposing observed-score variance into true differences among people, sampling of occasions, and classifier error, including a differential classifier functioning (DCF) component in which accuracy varies systematically across the people being measured. Analytic results are validated in simulation under constant and differential classifier functioning, and the framework is applied in a designed experiment over scoring configurations (prompts, models, aggregation choices) on a corpus of classroom transcripts, yielding a scalar selection criterion — projected construct-relevant reliability — for choosing among candidate LLM scoring systems before deployment.

## Translational abstract

Companies and schools are starting to use AI language models to score what people do — rating recorded lessons, classifying conversations, coding written responses. Before trusting those scores, most check only whether the AI agrees with human experts. But agreement isn't enough: an AI can match humans on average and still produce scores too noisy, or too systematically skewed, to fairly compare one person to another. This study asks when AI-produced scores can be trusted to measure human behavior, using classroom observations of teachers as the test case. It shows how to separate what the scores capture about real differences between teachers from noise and from the AI's own errors — including errors that hit some teachers harder than others — and provides a single criterion for choosing among candidate AI scoring systems before deploying them. The same approach applies anywhere AI is used to score people: evaluating service interactions, moderating content, or screening interviews.

## What this study does

I develop a measurement model for scores built by applying a fixed LLM classifier to counts of behaviors across occasions — here, teachers' instructional moves across lessons. The framework extends generalizability theory to the distinctive features of an LLM rater: unlike human raters, an LLM applies the *same* systematic scoring tendencies every time, so its errors cannot be averaged away by sampling more raters. The paper:

- Derives the **reliability coefficient** for classifier-based prevalence scores, decomposing observed-score variance into true differences among people, sampling of occasions, and classifier error — including a **differential classifier functioning (DCF)** component in which the classifier's accuracy varies systematically across the people being measured.
- Validates the analytic results in **simulation studies** under constant and differential classifier functioning.
- Applies the framework in a **designed experiment over scoring configurations** (prompts, models, aggregation choices) on a corpus of classroom transcripts, introducing a scalar selection criterion — **projected construct-relevant reliability** — for choosing among candidate LLM scoring systems before deploying them.
